description: Resolves the apparent contradiction between increased wind speed and decreased natural avalanche activity during SSW windows. Three complementary lines of evidence: (1) trigger-budget accounting shows warming suppression dominates wind activation; (2) disaggregation by moisture type reveals selective wet-slab collapse with preserved dry-slab activity; (3) effective snow transport is attenuated by reduced fresh-snow supply during cold-dry SSW regimes.

wind_offset_test.interpretation: Dry-slab natural avalanches (RR=1.122) are dramatically less suppressed than wet-slab (RR=0.201), a +92 percentage-point differential. This is consistent with wind-loading partially sustaining dry-slab activity. However, the massive wet-slab suppression (-80%) — driven by the elimination of warming and rain-on-snow triggers — dominates the overall budget.

verdict.interpretation: Wind transport potential (u³) increases by +25.4% during SSW windows, but 3-day fresh-snow supply changes by +24.7%. The effective transport (u³ × √snow) changes by +31.0%. Even where wind increases, the cold-dry SSW regime can limit the supply of transportable surface snow, attenuating the real-world impact of higher wind speeds on slab formation.

resolution.paradox: SSW windows show increased wind speed/transport, yet natural avalanche activity decreases overall
key_findings: Wind speed increases +12.8% (transport potential +25.4%) during SSW windows
resolution.resolution_mechanism:
The paradox is resolved by three complementary arguments:

1. TRIGGER-WEIGHT ASYMMETRY: Wind transport accounts for only ~12% of natural-release trigger weight. Even a large wind increase has limited leverage against the ~88% from warming, new-snow, rain-on-snow, and solar triggers — all of which are suppressed during SSW cold-dry windows.

2. SLAB-TYPE DISAGGREGATION: When avalanches are split by moisture type, dry-slab naturals (wind-slab candidates) actually increase (+12%), confirming wind-loading does work. But wet-slab naturals collapse (-80%) because their triggers (warming, rain) are eliminated. The wet-slab collapse dominates the overall decrease.

3. TRANSPORT ≠ WIND SPEED: Actual snow transport requires both wind AND available loose/fresh snow. The cold-dry SSW regime reduces fresh snowfall availability, attenuating the real-world impact of higher wind speeds (effective transport Δ = +31.0% vs raw wind potential Δ = +25.4%).
resolution.manuscript_sentence: Although SSW windows increase surface wind speed (+12.8%, p=0.0013), wind-slab loading accounts for only ~12% of natural-release triggers. Disaggregating by moisture type reveals that dry-slab avalanches (wind-slab candidates) are preserved (RR = 1.12), but wet-slab avalanches collapse (RR = 0.20, p = 0.05767) as warming events decrease -22.4%. The net weighted trigger change is +2.9% (95% CI: [-10.0, +16.8]), confirming that trigger suppression overwhelms the wind-loading signal.
